profiles.name: Cy Kendall
profiles.excerpt: Cy Kendall brought a deep voice and a screen specialty in policemen, officials and tough characters into the stock company of Lux Radio Theatre.
profiles.bio_html:
Cy Kendall was born Cyrus Willard Kendall in St. Louis in 1898 and became a prolific Hollywood character actor during the 1930s and 1940s. His heavy build and deep voice made him a natural choice for policemen, wardens, officials and underworld figures.

Radio used the same authority and edge that defined his screen work. Kendall appeared repeatedly in Lux Radio Theatre adaptations and also held continuing radio roles elsewhere, including Judge Carter on The Remarkable Miss Tuttle.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Kendall, documenting the radio side of a career that included more than a hundred screen appearances.

profiles.name: Ed Bishop
profiles.excerpt: Ed Bishop made Philip Marlowe one of his major radio roles, bringing an American voice to the BBC adaptations after establishing a long acting career in Britain.
profiles.bio_html:
Ed Bishop was born George Victor Bishop in Brooklyn in 1932 and settled professionally in Britain after studying drama. He became familiar to television audiences as Commander Ed Straker in UFO and as the voice of Captain Blue, while maintaining a substantial stage and radio career.

Radio gave Bishop one of his most durable literary roles when he played Philip Marlowe in BBC adaptations of Raymond Chandler's novels beginning in the 1970s. His American accent and restrained delivery suited Chandler's private detective without turning the character into parody.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 Philip Marlowe performances credited to Bishop and an additional BBC science-fiction radio performance, preserving a major microphone chapter of his British career.

profiles.name: Ferdinand Munier
profiles.excerpt: Ferdinand Munier carried decades of stage and screen character work into Lux Radio Theatre, where he became a dependable supporting player in Hollywood adaptations.
profiles.bio_html:
Ferdinand Munier was born in California in 1887 and developed a long career as a character actor through the silent and sound eras. His screen work repeatedly cast him as judges, doctors, officials, waiters and other instantly readable supporting figures.

Lux Radio Theatre used Munier in the same practical way, placing him around major guest stars in adaptations that needed experienced actors to establish small roles quickly and clearly. Surviving cast lists show him returning across multiple seasons.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Munier, documenting his place in the program's regular Hollywood supporting company.

profiles.name: Hal K. Dawson
profiles.excerpt: Hal K. Dawson was a prolific Hollywood character actor whose radio work ranged from Lux Radio Theatre to mystery and FBI drama.
profiles.bio_html:
Hal K. Dawson was born in Connecticut in 1896 and became one of Hollywood's busiest supporting actors. Beginning in the 1920s, he accumulated hundreds of film and television appearances, often as clerks, officials, businessmen and other sharply defined character parts.

Radio drew on the same dependable character technique. Dawson worked in Lux Radio Theatre, The Whistler, This Is Your FBI and Let George Do It, moving between prestige film adaptation and crime drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 12 Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Dawson, two each on The Whistler and This Is Your FBI, and an additional Let George Do It appearance.

profiles.name: Kevin McCarthy
profiles.excerpt: Kevin McCarthy returned repeatedly to radio drama late in his career, becoming a strong CBS Radio Mystery Theater repertory actor after decades on stage and screen.
profiles.bio_html:
Kevin McCarthy was born in Seattle in 1914 and built a long career across Broadway, film and television. He is especially remembered for starring in Invasion of the Body Snatchers, though his professional life extended far beyond that single film.

During the 1970s and 1980s McCarthy became a recurring performer on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, where his stage-trained delivery worked equally well in literary adaptation, mystery and supernatural drama. He also played Sherlock Holmes for the series.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to McCarthy, representing a substantial late-career return to dramatic radio.

profiles.name: Roland Winters
profiles.excerpt: Roland Winters combined radio announcing and acting before becoming the final regular film actor to portray Charlie Chan.
profiles.bio_html:
Roland Winters was born Roland Winternitz in Boston in 1904 and began acting onstage while still young. During the 1930s he also worked in Boston radio, including sports announcing for WNAC, before film became the more visible part of his career.

Winters continued in radio until the late 1940s, then succeeded Sidney Toler as Charlie Chan in six films. His earlier announcing work was substantial enough to remain a second professional branch alongside acting.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine This Is Your FBI performances credited to Winters, five Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances and additional work on Murder Clinic and The Shadow.

profiles.name: Arlene Walker
profiles.excerpt: Arlene Walker was a recurring Theater Five repertory actress during ABC radio drama’s 1960s revival.
profiles.bio_html:
Arlene Walker is best documented through the New York radio repertory of the 1960s. Her surviving credits place her repeatedly on Theater Five, ABC's weekday dramatic anthology during one of the final sustained attempts to keep network radio drama in regular production.

The series shifted constantly among suspense, domestic drama, crime and speculative stories, so recurring actors had to establish new characters quickly. Walker's repeated casting places her among the dependable players who gave that anthology its continuity.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 16 Theater Five performances credited to Walker, providing a concentrated record of her work in later network radio drama.

profiles.name: Barbara Weeks
profiles.excerpt: Barbara Weeks was a major daytime and dramatic radio actress whose surviving GRH work includes Barrie Craig and Inner Sanctum Mysteries.
profiles.bio_html:
Barbara Weeks was born in Binghamton, New York in 1906 and trained at the American Academy of Dramatic Arts. Radio became the center of her career, especially serial drama, where she was known for continuing roles including Her Honor, Nancy James and Young Doctor Malone.

Weeks also worked extensively outside daytime serials. Mystery and crime programs used her as a flexible dramatic actress, including Barrie Craig, Inner Sanctum Mysteries and Gang Busters.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves six Barrie Craig performances credited to Weeks, five Inner Sanctum Mysteries appearances and additional work on Gang Busters and Lux Radio Theatre.

profiles.name: Bernard Grant
profiles.excerpt: Bernard Grant was a durable New York radio and television actor whose microphone career stretched from Johnny Dollar and Theater Five into CBS Radio Mystery Theater.
profiles.bio_html:
Bernard Grant was born in 1920 and built a long acting career in New York across radio, stage and daytime television. He later became familiar to television audiences through continuing roles on Guiding Light and One Life to Live.

Radio remained an important part of that career across several decades. Grant appeared on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar and Theater Five before returning to dramatic broadcasting as a frequent CBS Radio Mystery Theater performer.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Theater Five performances credited to Grant, three Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, two CBS Radio Mystery Theater broadcasts and additional work on Crime and Peter Chambers and Top Secret.

profiles.name: Charlotte Holland
profiles.excerpt: Charlotte Holland was a Canadian-born radio actress whose surviving work is strongest in Inner Sanctum Mysteries and wartime dramatic anthology.
profiles.bio_html:
Charlotte Holland was born in Canada in 1915 and worked professionally in radio and theatre before later settling in Britain with her husband, actor and director Sam Wanamaker. Her radio credits place her firmly inside the New York dramatic repertory of the 1940s and 1950s.

Holland appeared repeatedly on Inner Sanctum Mysteries and also worked on Words at War, The Mysterious Traveler, Broadway Is My Beat and Columbia Workshop. Those programs ranged from wartime literature to supernatural and crime drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves nine Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances credited to Holland, three Words at War appearances, two The Mysterious Traveler broadcasts and additional anthology work.
